pages.title: 03 — Edge Vocabulary
pages.body:
# 03 — Edge Vocabulary

The intellectual work is not "relation / effect / action" — those are categories. The work is **enumerating the verbs**, and keeping the list brutally short.

Every authored edge type is a tax somebody pays forever.

## Split by who produces it

### Derived — free, be generous

Extracted from the AST, git history, and build config. Costs nothing per edge, so the vocabulary can be wide.

```
calls · imports · produces · consumes · exposes · touched_by
```

### Authored — expensive, cap at five

Requires a human. This list should be treated as closed.

```
implements · part_of · constrained_by · supersedes · related_to
```

## On `related_to`

It is the escape hatch and it will swallow a large share of usage. That is fine, and it is informative.

When `related_to` starts dominating, look at what is inside it. The frequency distribution tells you which real edge type is missing.

**Let the vocabulary grow from evidence, not from a design session.**

## Language vs norms

- A **language** is enforced — grammar, validator, things that fail
- A **norm** is social — convention, degrades gracefully

Languages give guarantees but demand tooling before delivering any value. Norms deliver value on day one and decay without enforcement.

The workable shape is **a thin language wrapping a thick norm**: closed vocabulary, open prose. Edge types are enumerated and validated. Everything else is human text.

## Enforcement

A norm without a linter has a half-life of roughly six weeks.

- JSON Schema over the frontmatter — unknown edge type fails CI
- Entity registry with aliases — `login-page` and `user-login-page` resolve to one node
- PR check — a story branch with a dangling entity reference fails

About a day of work. It is the difference between a living graph and a directory of files nobody trusts.

## Entity identity

If entity names are free text, one concept becomes four nodes within a month and the graph quietly stops working.

Decide what an entity *is* — domain concept, code artifact, or screen. Hedging across all three is fine on a whiteboard and fatal in a schema.

pages.title: 04 — Asserted vs Suggested Edges
pages.body:
# 04 — Asserted vs Suggested Edges

## The hard rule

**Cosine similarity never creates an edge.**

Closeness is not meaning. Two things can embed near each other and be unrelated. Two things can be tightly coupled and embed far apart. An edge built on distance is a guess wearing the costume of a fact.

Similarity is symmetric and untyped. Relations are directional and typed. They are not the same object.

## But inference still has a role

Most content across an organisation is never explicitly linked. Nobody puts the Confluence page ID in the JIRA story. If the system only ever shows authored edges, it stays empty across most of the estate.

The resolution is not to ban inference. It is to **mark it**.

## Two edge classes

### Asserted

Declared by a human or derived from git/AST. Trusted. Used as fact.

### Suggested

Proposed by semantic similarity. A **candidate, not a fact.** Carries a confidence tier. Visibly distinct in every surface that shows it.

## Promotion

A human promotes a suggestion to asserted with one action. It then becomes trusted.

This is the correct division of labour:

> Semantics does not draw the graph. It **proposes drafts of edges** for a human to confirm.

The bootstrap value is real — it links across sources that nobody connected by hand — without contaminating the asserted layer.

## Why this matters downstream

An agent consuming context must be able to tell the difference. "This service calls that one" and "this page probably relates to that story" cannot arrive looking identical. The first is a fact to build on; the second is a lead to check.

pages.title: 05 — Confidence Scoring
pages.body:
# 05 — Confidence Scoring

## What it is

Every edge carries a confidence tier reflecting **how it was established**, not how strong a similarity score was.

| Origin | Tier |
|---|---|
| Git-derived or human-declared | Highest |
| Explicit JIRA link someone typed | High |
| Semantic candidate across sources | Moderate, labelled inferred |

## Primary use — ranking

The tiering *is* the ranking function. High-confidence structured context surfaces first. Semantic guesses come after. The consuming agent can see which is which.

## Secondary use — a mirror

The more valuable framing, and the one to put in front of leadership:

> The score is a measurement of the organisation's documentation health.

If retrieval is dominated by low-confidence semantic guesses, that is not a tooling failure. It is the system reporting that the documentation is disconnected.

The same number that ranks results becomes a **quality metric that can be driven down over time**. Better linking → higher confidence → better agent output. That is a roadmap handed to leadership, not just a feature.

## The trap

**Do not present the number as precise.**

A cosine similarity of 0.82 is not "82% probability of a real relation." It is a distance.

Bucket into high / medium / low. Do not show decimals. The moment three decimal places appear on a screen, someone treats it as truth — and that recreates exactly the problem the whole design exists to avoid.

## Tuning from evidence

Thresholds should not be guessed. See [11 — The Feedback Loop](11-feedback-loop.md): promotion and rejection events give per-source accuracy data, and thresholds follow from that.

pages.title: 06 — Source Characteristics
pages.body:
# 06 — Source Characteristics

Organisational documentation spans sources with very different structural character. Each needs a different extraction strategy. Treating them uniformly is the mistake.

## Bitbucket / code — most structured

Services in a known language. Edges available from calls, imports, and the config portal that wires services together.

**Fully derivable.** No authoring required for the bulk of it.

**Day-one caveat:** a new project with a single service has almost no edges. The graph is thin — correctly so. There is nothing to infer; there is simply not much there yet. It grows as the project grows.

## JIRA — partially structured

Some native structure (issue links, epics), but **most stories are never linked to code**, because linking is optional and nobody enforces it.

So JIRA needs both:
- **Graph edges** where links exist, or where branch → PR → files derivation works
- **Semantic candidates** where they do not

This is the source where inference earns the most.

## Confluence — genuinely unstructured

Prose. No native edges at all. The best documentation store per project, and the least connected.

Pure semantic territory. Its value is realised by proposing links *into* the structured layer: this page appears to relate to these stories, which relate to this service.

## The bridging pattern

```
Confluence page  ──semantic──▶  JIRA stories  ──derived──▶  code entities
   (unstructured)   (suggested)    (partial)    (asserted)    (structured)
```

Semantic search builds the bridge from unstructured content into the structured graph. Everything it proposes is a **suggested** edge until promoted — see [04](04-asserted-vs-suggested-edges.md).

## Implication for adapters

The existing adapter design (`CodeSource`, `TicketSource`, `DocSource`) already matches this split. Extraction strategy should be a property of the adapter, not of the core.

pages.title: 07 — Why Graph First
pages.body:
# 07 — Why Graph First

## Why vector RAG is the default everywhere

Not because it is the best available structure. Because it is the most **generally applicable** one.

1. **The canonical case had no structure.** RAG was developed for open-domain QA over prose — encyclopaedias, support tickets, policy PDFs. There are no `calls` edges in a benefits handbook. Chunk-and-embed is not a compromise there; it is the only option.

2. **Vectors need zero authoring.** Point at a folder, get semantic search, model nothing. Knowledge graphs had their run — the Semantic Web, RDF, OWL — and largely failed at scale for one reason: someone must author the ontology, and that person is not the one who collects the benefit.

3. **A tooling flywheel locked it in.** An industry formed around the vector-shaped answer. "RAG" became synonymous with "embed and retrieve" through repetition, not demonstration.

Graph-based RAG does exist and is active work. It is less visible because it cannot be packaged as a drop-in — it has to be modelled per domain.

## Why this project should depart from the default

Three conditions, rare together:

1. **The corpus is pre-structured.** AST, git, issue links. The graph is largely *derivable*, not authorable — which dodges the exact failure mode that killed the Semantic Web.

2. **The questions are structural.** What calls this. What breaks if I change it. Why was this decided. Vector search answers these approximately when an exact answer exists.

3. **Wrong answers are expensive.** A near-miss in a chatbot is a bad paragraph. A near-miss in a PR review at a bank is a defect in production. Approximate retrieval is a much worse deal when precision is load-bearing.

> General solutions are correct when you do not know your domain. This domain is known — the node types, edge types, and question shapes are all known. The generality tax buys nothing.

## Practical consequence

Phase 1 is graph-first. Entities, edges, stories, decisions, references in MongoDB, with `$graphLookup` for bounded traversal — avoiding the need to justify a new graph database to a platform team.

This removes the embedding service and the external embeddings dependency from Phase 1: one fewer external API, one fewer key to manage, one fewer item in a security review.

## The asymmetry that justifies the order

Adding vector search later is **additive** — new collection, new index, existing queries untouched.

Getting the entity schema wrong is a **migration**.

Spend the foundation budget on the graph model; keep retrieval swappable behind an interface.

## Honest risk

Graph-first makes the system dependent on the graph being populated, which makes git-derived edge extraction load-bearing rather than merely clever.

If derivation underperforms, the result is a system that is excellent on a small share of the estate and blind on the rest — where a vector-first build would have been mediocre everywhere. Mediocre-everywhere is sometimes the right shape for a first deployment.

**This should be decided deliberately, after testing derivation on a real repository.**

pages.title: 08 — The Role of Vectors
pages.body:
# 08 — The Role of Vectors

Vectors help you **reach into** the graph. They never define what is in it.

## What embeddings cannot do

A retrieval embedding and a model's internal embeddings live in **different vector spaces**. A 1024-dim retrieval vector is trained so similar documents land near each other under cosine distance. A model's input embedding layer is trained so tokens land where the rest of its parameters expect them.

They are not translations of each other. There is no way to hand a model a retrieval vector and have it skip tokenisation.

**The retrieval vector never enters the model.** It is a lookup key and nothing else. What crosses into the model is always plain text.

So embedding cost is *added*, never saved. This kills "efficiency of representation" as a justification for RAG, and that justification deserves to be killed.

## What RAG actually buys

**Selection under a context budget.** With a thousand stories, they cannot all fit in the window. The job is answering *which ten go in*.

Not compression. Not cheaper representation. Selection.

Once that is accepted, the design question stops being "how do we store context" and becomes "**how do we pick well**" — a much better question, and one the graph answers more precisely than similarity does.

## Three legitimate roles

### 1. As a property on a node

An embedding stored *on* an entity, enabling fuzzy English → node lookup. A query like "how do we handle bad passwords on sign-in" matches no literal entity name; something must bridge it.

At modest scale there is a cheaper bridge: a few hundred entity names and one-line descriptions fit comfortably in a prompt. Asking the model to pick outperforms cosine similarity, because it reasons about the question rather than matching surface form.

### 2. As the floor for unmodelled territory

The graph knows only what was authored or derived. Point it at a service nobody has modelled and it returns **nothing** — and an empty answer is the worst answer, because the agent proceeds blind.

Vector search over raw chunks returns *something*. Degraded, unranked by structure, but non-zero.

```
Graph  → sharp, curated, grows slowly
Vector → dumb, complete, covers everything from day one
```

### 3. As a proposer of candidate edges

Semantic similarity across sources generates **suggested** edges for human promotion. See [04](04-asserted-vs-suggested-edges.md).

## Scoping, not replacing

Joining every story attached to a long-lived entity re-creates the original problem — a blown context window.

The graph **scopes** retrieval rather than replacing it:

```
query → entity resolution → bounded graph traversal
      → candidate set (~40 items, not 1000)
      → rank within candidates → top-k → context
```

Search stops being a scan over the whole corpus and becomes a ranker over a structurally justified subset. Where a wrong answer is at least *related*.

## When to add it

Log every query resolving to zero or wrong nodes.

- Failures dominated by "content existed but nothing linked to it" → semantic fallback is earning its place
- Failures dominated by "nobody modelled that" → the answer is authoring, and embeddings would not have helped

pages.title: 09 — Authoring Cost
pages.body:
# 09 — Authoring Cost

## The failure mode

Ontology projects rarely fail because the ontology is bad. They fail because **authoring is a cost paid by one person and the benefit is collected by someone else, later, invisibly.**

Any design that requires every analyst to fill in a "related entities" field is asking for work whose payoff the author never feels. It will be filled in for two months and abandoned.

This is the single largest risk to the whole approach.

## Three ways to get edges, by cost

### 1. Authored at story creation
A field in the ticket. Reliable, and the most expensive. Depends entirely on discipline that erodes.

### 2. Inferred by a model at ingest, human-confirmed
Cheaper. Noisier. Produces suggested edges (see [04](04-asserted-vs-suggested-edges.md)).

### 3. Derived from git — the strongest option

A story has a branch. A branch has a PR. A PR touches files. Files map to entities.

```
VS1 → LoginController.java, LoginValidator.java → login-page
```

This falls out of history that already exists. No new human work at all.

**Why it is unusually clean here:** the existing SOP is already *one story, one branch, one PR*, with feedback arriving as new commits on the same branch. That discipline — adopted for unrelated reasons — makes the story→code linkage far cleaner than at most organisations.

That accidental alignment is worth a great deal, and it is what makes graph-first defensible rather than aspirational.

## The shift it produces

> The graph builds itself from work already done. Human curation becomes **correction, not authoring.**

Correcting a wrong edge is a fraction of the cost of creating a right one, and the feedback is immediate. That is a cost profile people actually sustain.

## The open validation

Everything above is reasoning, not evidence.

**Before the architecture hardens: test git-derived edge extraction on one real repository.** Measure what fraction of stories map cleanly to entities and how much noise the mapping carries.

If derivation holds, graph-first is right. If it does not, revisit [07](07-why-graph-first.md) — a vector-first Phase 1 with graph layered on later becomes the safer shape.

## Keeping the authored layer thin

The same principle applies throughout:

- Dependencies → derived. Reference nodes → authored, only where a decision attaches.
- Code edges → derived, generous. Semantic edges → authored vocabulary, capped at five.

Every layer keeps the free part wide and the human part narrow.

pages.body:
# 10 — Storage Format

## Do not invent syntax

This is where these projects die. Someone designs a notation, then spends the project writing a parser for it instead of building the thing.

The consumer here is an LLM. It reads semi-structured text natively. **No parser is needed to make context legible — only a convention to make it consistent.**

Use a boring carrier that already has tooling.

## The shape

YAML frontmatter in Markdown:

```markdown
---
context-spec: v1
entity: user-login-page
type: screen
edges:
  - implements: VS1
  - implements: CSS1
  - persists_to: credential-store
  - constrained_by: DEC-014
---

## What this is
The authenticated entry point...

## Why it is this way
Third-party login was deferred (see DEC-014) because...
```

Free parsers everywhere. Renders in every viewer. Git-diffable. Readable by a model with no preprocessing.

**Structure lives in the frontmatter. Irreplaceable human knowledge lives in the prose below it.**

## Reference nodes carry parameters

A bare name is under-specified in ways that cause defects. "Uses SHA-256" invites a fast-hash password implementation, which is a security defect — the real usage is almost certainly PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, correct and FIPS-approved, casually shortened in speech.

A human colleague disambiguates automatically. An agent does not.

```yaml
entity: pbkdf2-hmac-sha256
type: reference
aliases: [PBKDF2, "SHA-256 hashing", sha256]
parameters:
  iterations: 600000
  salt_bytes: 16
  key_length: 256
authority: org-security-standard
prohibitions:
  - Never use bare SHA-256/MessageDigest for password storage — fast hash, GPU-crackable
constrained_by: DEC-014
```

### On `prohibitions`

Half the value of an architectural reference is not what to do — it is **what people keep doing wrong.** That knowledge lives in senior heads and evaporates. It is cheap to write once.

## Version from line one

`context-spec: v1` in every file.

The vocabulary will be wrong at first — it always is. The difference between a painful migration and an impossible one is knowing which files were written under which rules.

## The adoption constraint

The whole specification — vocabulary, format, rules — should fit on **one page**.

If it does not fit on one page, it will not be adopted.

## Reverse traversal

Structured parameters enable the query that sells this internally:

> Every service in the estate using PBKDF2 with fewer than 600,000 iterations.

Crypto deprecations, TLS floors, eventually post-quantum migration — all reverse-index problems. Agent context is the day-to-day benefit that keeps the graph fresh; **audit and dependency agility** is the benefit that justifies it upward.

pages.title: 11 — The Feedback Loop
pages.body:
# 11 — The Feedback Loop

## The loop

```
semantic proposes  →  human promotes or rejects  →  signal captured
                                                          │
                             thresholds tuned  ◀───────────┘
```

Every promotion and every rejection is training data about *this* estate.

## What it gives you

**Per-source accuracy.** Over time the promote/reject record shows how well inference performs from Confluence, from JIRA, from code comments — separately. Thresholds can then be set from evidence rather than guessed.

**A number that improves.** The share of retrieved context that is high-confidence rises as the graph fills in. That is a metric that trends in the right direction, which is what keeps a project funded.

**Compounding value.** Each correction makes the next retrieval better. The system gets more useful the longer it is used — unlike a static index, which is exactly as good on day 400 as on day 1.

## Why this is not model training

Worth being precise, because the framing is appealing and easy to overstate.

Nothing here changes model weights. What accumulates is **a project-specific knowledge structure** the model reads at query time. The learning is in the graph, not in the model.

That distinction is a feature, not a limitation:

- Inspectable — every edge has a visible origin
- Reversible — a wrong edge is deleted, not retrained away
- Portable — the graph outlives any particular model
- Attributable — answers trace to sources

A fine-tuned model cannot offer any of those.

## Capture requirements

For the loop to work, record on every promotion or rejection:

- The proposed edge and its origin source pair
- The confidence tier at proposal time
- The decision and who made it
- Timestamp

This is small, cheap, and must exist from the first version. Retrofitting it means discarding the first months of signal.

## The framing that lands

> This is a learning pipeline for your own estate. It does not get smarter about software in general — it gets smarter about *your* software, and it shows its work.

pages.body:
# ContextRAG — Design Position Paper (v2)

**Status:** Concept stage. No implementation started. Revised after external critical evaluation of v1.

**Context:** A tech lead / solution architect at a bank is building a context retrieval system so AI coding agents can work with real understanding of an existing software estate. This document consolidates the design reasoning and the revisions forced by review.

**Reading note:** Sections 9, 10, and 11 contain the unresolved parts. Sections 2–7 are settled and one claim (Section 2) has now been independently verified.

---

## 0. What changed from v1

| # | Finding | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | v1 claimed git-derivation meant "no new human work." False — `file → entity` is not derivable. | Section 9 rewritten. Authoring cost is owned, not dissolved. |
| 2 | v1 removed embeddings from Phase 1 while calling the vector floor load-bearing. Self-contradiction. | Section 8 now states the floor explicitly and identifies it as **asymmetric**. |
| 3 | Stale asserted edges are confident lies. Freshness was deferred entirely. | Provenance and staleness now schema-level from v1 (Section 4.6). |
| 4 | Traversal semantics over suggested edges were unspecified. | Section 6 now specifies: traverse asserted only; suggested apply at ranking. |
| 5 | "The questions are structural" was introspection, never measured. | Moved from premise to **hypothesis under test** (Section 10). |
| 6 | v1's own worked example used `persists_to`, a verb in neither vocabulary list. | Vocabulary revised (Section 4.2) — the fix is a wider *derived* set, not a bigger authored one. |
| 7 | Every "a human then does X" is an unowned cost. | Section 12 — named owners required, or the step does not happen. |
| 8 | Validation gate measured the wrong things. | Section 10 rewritten around three gates, not one. |
| 9 | Prior art unexamined. | Section 13 added. Aider's repo map materially changes the build estimate. |
| 10 | Neither v1 nor the review addressed whether the agent will *query well*. | Section 11 added — the largest unaddressed gap. |
| 11 | Validation planned in the environment where the design helps least. | Section 10 — validate against a mature repository, not greenfield. |

---

## 1. The problem

When a human tech lead works with AI coding agents at speed, context evaporates. Decisions scatter, architecture intent degrades, each session starts cold.

Observed concretely: a self-hosted model with access to repositories, Confluence, and JIRA still produced generic output. The failure was **not hallucination** — it was genericness. The model reached the data without understanding how any of it related.

Two constraints followed:

1. **Reaching ≠ understanding.** Access does not produce ecosystem awareness.
2. **Token limits rule out brute force.** Loading whole repositories exhausts the window before the task begins.

Single-service work is tolerable today. Multi-service work breaks down — the agent understands one service's code but not the contracts between services, the topics, or the decisions constraining the current change.

---

## 2. What RAG buys — and what it does not

**Verified in review.** Retrieval embeddings and a model's input embeddings occupy **different vector spaces**. A retrieval vector is trained so similar documents cluster under cosine distance; a model's embedding layer is trained so tokens land where the rest of its parameters expect them. They are not translations of each other, and there is no deployable path for handing a model a retrieval vector to skip tokenisation.

The retrieval vector therefore **never enters the model**. It is a lookup key. What crosses the boundary is always plain text, tokenised normally. Embedding cost is *added*, never saved.

This eliminates "efficient representation" as a justification for RAG.

**What remains is the real justification: selection under a context budget.** With a thousand stories, they cannot all fit. RAG's only job is answering *which ten go in*.

The design question is therefore not "how do we store context" but **"how do we pick well."**

---

## 3. The core reframing: context as a graph

Context is not a pile of text. It is **a set of nodes and edges** — entities and the typed, directional relations between them.

Chunk-embed-retrieve is correct for corpora with no structure. A software estate is the opposite: it has an AST, commit history, issue links, config wiring. The relations already exist and are machine-extractable. Applying a technique built for structureless prose discards that structure and then approximates it back with similarity.

### Design by constraint, not design by prompt

- **Design by prompt:** hand the model everything, hope it infers the relations.
- **Design by constraint:** supply the relations.

This is the thesis, and the precise diagnosis of the observed failure.

**Consequence:** the unit of context is the **entity**, not the chunk. Chunks attach to entities. This is a foundation-level commitment — cheap now, a migration later.

---

## 4. The model

### 4.1 Three node classes

| Class | Character | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Entities** | Internal, mutable, hold *current truth* | `login-page`, `credential-store` |
| **Events** — stories, decisions | Historical, immutable once closed | `VS1`, `CSS1`, `DEC-014` |
| **References** | External, stable, owned by nobody | `PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256`, `OAuth2`, `Kafka` |

Reference nodes have a property the others lack: **the model already knows what they are.** They must not document the algorithm — they document *this organisation's use of it*. That keeps them small enough to afford.

**Temporal separation** answers "what did we use before, and why did we change?":

| Question | Answered by |
|---|---|
| What does it use now? | Entity |
| When did that change? | Story |
| Why did it change? | Decision |

Reference edges attach to the **entity**, not the story — otherwise current truth requires replaying history.

**Boundary test** (without it, every library becomes a node):

> A reference node exists only if someone could reasonably ask **"why this one?"** — or if getting it wrong is a defect.

Argon2id vs PBKDF2 qualifies. `commons-lang3` does not.

### 4.2 Edge vocabulary — revised

v1 declared five authored verbs closed, then used a sixth (`persists_to`) in its own first example. The instructive part is *which* verb: `persists_to` is largely derivable from code — repository interfaces, DAO wiring, connection config. The example did not prove the authored set is too small. It proved the **derived set was too narrow**, pushing derivable facts into the authored budget.

**Derived — free, be generous** (AST, git, build and runtime config):
```
calls · imports · produces · consumes · exposes
persists_to · reads_from · configured_by · touched_by
```

**Authored — expensive, capped at five, treated as closed:**
```
implements · part_of · constrained_by · supersedes · related_to
```

The discipline: **before adding an authored verb, prove it cannot be derived.** Most candidates fail that test.

`related_to` remains the escape hatch and will absorb a large share of usage. Its contents reveal which real verb is missing — but only if someone reads them. See Section 12; this is an owned task, not an aspiration.

### 4.3 Language versus norms

A **language** is enforced — grammar, validator, things that fail. A **norm** is social — degrades gracefully. Languages demand tooling before delivering value; norms deliver immediately and decay without enforcement.

The workable shape: **a thin language wrapping a thick norm.** Closed validated vocabulary, open human prose.

### 4.4 Storage format

**Do not invent syntax.** This is where such projects die — someone designs a notation and spends the project writing a parser.

The consumer is an LLM, which reads semi-structured text natively. No parser is needed to make context legible, only a convention to make it consistent.

```markdown
---
context-spec: v1
entity: user-login-page
type: screen
files:                      # the mapping that is NOT derivable — see §9
  - src/main/java/**/LoginController.java
  - src/main/java/**/LoginValidator.java
  - src/main/resources/templates/login.html
edges:
  - implements: VS1
  - constrained_by: DEC-014
provenance:                 # see §4.6
  last_verified_sha: a3f9c21
  last_verified_at: 2026-08-01
---

## What this is
The authenticated entry point...

## Why it is this way
Third-party login was deferred (see DEC-014) because...
```

YAML frontmatter in Markdown. Free parsers, git-diffable, renders anywhere, model-readable with no preprocessing. **Structure in the frontmatter; irreplaceable human knowledge in the prose.**

Reference nodes carry parameters, because a bare name causes defects:

```yaml
entity: pbkdf2-hmac-sha256
type: reference
aliases: [PBKDF2, "SHA-256 hashing", sha256]
parameters:
  iterations: 600000
  salt_bytes: 16
  key_length: 256
authority: org-security-standard
prohibitions:
  - Never use bare SHA-256/MessageDigest for password storage — fast hash, GPU-crackable
constrained_by: DEC-014
```

The motivating case: "credential store uses SHA-256" is dangerously under-specified. An agent given that will plausibly write `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")` for password storage — a security defect, since SHA-256 is deliberately *fast* and GPU-crackable at scale. The real implementation is almost certainly PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (correct, FIPS-approved), casually shortened in speech. A human colleague disambiguates automatically; an agent does not.

`prohibitions` encodes what people repeatedly get *wrong* — knowledge that lives in senior heads, evaporates on attrition, cheap to write once.

**Version from line one** (`context-spec: v1`). The vocabulary will be wrong initially; the difference between a painful and an impossible migration is knowing which files followed which rules.

### 4.5 Enforcement and entity identity

A norm without a linter has a half-life of roughly six weeks in a large organisation.

- JSON Schema over frontmatter — unknown edge type fails CI
- Entity registry with aliases — `login-page` and `user-login-page` resolve to one node
- PR check — dangling entity references fail the branch

**Entity identity is a real hazard.** If names are free text, one concept becomes four nodes within a month and the graph quietly stops working. What an entity *is* — domain concept, code artifact, or screen — must be decided. Hedging across all three is fine on a whiteboard and fatal in a schema.

**Adoption constraint:** the author-facing spec must fit on one page. This paper is *not* that page — it is the rationale. The one-pager is a separate artifact and should be written first; this document is its appendix, not the reverse.

### 4.6 Provenance and staleness — new in v2

The trust model says asserted edges are used as fact. Therefore **a stale asserted edge is a confident lie** — worse than a suggested edge and worse than no edge, because the agent builds on it without checking. A graph wrong about current truth actively causes the defects the design exists to prevent.

Required in the schema from v1, even if enforcement lands later:

- `last_verified_sha` — the commit at which this edge was confirmed
- `last_verified_at` — timestamp
- **Merge hook** — a merged PR refreshes edges for the entities whose files it touched; everything else ages
- **Aging policy** — an unverified edge past a threshold is demoted from asserted to stale, and surfaces to the agent as such

Demotion rather than deletion, because a stale edge is still a lead. The failure to avoid is presenting it as current.

---

## 5. Sources have different structural character

Extraction strategy belongs to the adapter, not the core.

**Code repositories — most structured.** Edges from calls, imports, and config wiring services together. Fully derivable at the *file* level. *Day-one caveat:* a new project with one service has almost no edges — correctly thin.

**Ticket system (JIRA) — partially structured.** Some native links, but most stories are never linked to code because linking is optional and unenforced. Needs derived edges where links exist, semantic candidates where they do not. Where inference earns most.

**Wiki (Confluence) — genuinely unstructured.** Prose, no native edges, simultaneously the best per-project documentation store and the least connected. Its value is realised by proposing links *into* the structured layer.

```
Confluence page  ──semantic──▶  JIRA stories  ──derived──▶  code entities
  (unstructured)   (suggested)     (partial)    (asserted)    (structured)
```

---

## 6. Asserted versus suggested edges

### The hard rule

**Cosine similarity never creates an edge.**

Closeness is not meaning. Two things can embed near each other and be unrelated; two things can be tightly coupled and embed far apart. An edge built on distance is a guess wearing the costume of a fact.

Similarity is symmetric and untyped. Relations are directional and typed. Collapsing them discards the exact property that makes a graph better than similarity search.

### But inference still has a role

Most content is never explicitly linked. A system showing only authored edges stays empty across most of the estate. The resolution is not to ban inference but to **mark it**.

| Class | Origin | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Asserted** | Human-declared or git/AST-derived | Trusted, used as fact |
| **Suggested** | Semantic similarity | Candidate with a confidence tier, visibly distinct |
| **Stale** | Asserted, past verification threshold | Surfaced as a lead, never as current truth |

> Semantics does not draw the graph. It **proposes drafts of edges** for a human to confirm.

### Traversal semantics — new in v2

Storing both classes in one collection is fine. The decision that actually matters is whether traversal *follows* suggested edges. Follow them and inferred guesses contaminate the scoping step that justifies the whole candidate set; skip them and coverage collapses to the asserted skeleton.

**Specified:** bounded traversal follows **asserted edges only**. Suggested edges apply at the **final ranking stage** as one-hop annotations on already-selected candidates.

Rationale: scoping must be defensible; ranking may be probabilistic. This determines what "bounded traversal" returns and therefore belongs in the schema, not in implementation.

---

## 7. Confidence scoring

Every edge carries a tier reflecting **how it was established**, not how high a similarity score was.

| Origin | Tier |
|---|---|
| Git-derived or human-declared, recently verified | Highest |
| Explicit ticket link someone typed | High |
| Asserted but stale | Medium, flagged |
| Semantic candidate across sources | Moderate, labelled inferred |

**Primary use — ranking.** The tiering *is* the ranking function.

**Secondary use — a mirror.** The framing for leadership:

> The score measures the organisation's documentation health.

If retrieval is dominated by low-confidence guesses, that is the system reporting that the documentation is disconnected. The same number that ranks results becomes a quality metric to drive down. Better linking → higher confidence → better agent output.

*Caveat added in v2:* this framing is untested against anyone who would actually be measured by it. A metric that makes teams look bad can be resisted rather than acted on. Treat it as a hypothesis about organisational behaviour, not a certainty.

**The trap.** A cosine similarity of 0.82 is not "82% probability of a real relation" — it is a distance. Bucket into high/medium/low; show no decimals. The moment three decimals appear on a screen, someone treats them as truth.

### The feedback loop

```
semantic proposes → human promotes or rejects → signal captured
                                                      │
                          thresholds tuned ◀──────────┘
```

Recorded per event: proposed edge and source pair, tier at proposal, decision, actor, timestamp. Small, cheap, and required from v1 — retrofitting discards the first months of signal.

**This is not model training.** No weights change. What accumulates is a project-specific knowledge structure read at query time. The learning is in the graph — which is a feature: inspectable, reversible, portable, attributable. A fine-tuned model offers none of these.

---

## 8. Why graph-first — and what the floor is

### Why vector RAG is the default

Not because it is best, but because it is most **generally applicable**.

1. **The canonical case had no structure.** RAG was developed for QA over prose. There are no `calls` edges in a benefits handbook.
2. **Vectors need zero authoring.** Knowledge graphs had their era — Semantic Web, RDF, OWL — and largely failed at scale because someone must author the ontology and that person is not the beneficiary.
3. **A tooling flywheel locked it in.** "RAG" became synonymous with "embed and retrieve" through repetition rather than demonstration.

### Why this project may justifiably depart

1. **The corpus is pre-structured.** AST, git, issue links. Much of the graph is *derivable*.
2. **The questions are structural** — *now demoted to hypothesis; see Section 10.*
3. **Wrong answers are expensive.** A near-miss in a chatbot is a bad paragraph. A near-miss in a bank's PR review is a defect in production.

### The floor — corrected in v2

v1 called the vector floor load-bearing ("empty is the worst answer, because the agent proceeds blind") and then removed embeddings from Phase 1. That was a contradiction.

The resolution is that **the floor is asymmetric**, and neither v1 nor the review stated this precisely:

| Content | Floor without ContextRAG | Adequate? |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | Agent's own grep and file reads | Yes — for a personal build |
| **Decisions, wiki prose, ticket history** | *Nothing* | **No** |

So Phase 1 without embeddings is not uniformly blind. It is blind on exactly the content that has **no other retrieval path** — which is where the irreplaceable "why" lives.

Two consequences:

1. **Text search over prose sources belongs in Phase 1**, even if vector search does not. Lexical search on decisions and wiki content is cheap and closes the real gap.
2. **The code floor assumption inverts at the office boundary.** A personal build with Claude Code has full repo access. A constrained office CLI with a time budget may not. What is a safe assumption at home is a risk at work, and must be re-tested before deployment.

### The role vectors retain

1. **As a property on a node** — fuzzy English → node lookup. *Note:* at a few hundred entities, names plus one-line descriptions fit in a prompt, and model selection may outperform cosine similarity. Embeddings may not be needed even here — but see the cost caveat in Section 11.
2. **As the floor for unmodelled prose** — degraded, unranked, non-zero.
3. **As a proposer of candidate edges** (Section 6).

### Scoping, not replacing

```
query → entity resolution → bounded traversal (asserted only)
      → candidate set (~40 items, not 1000)
      → rank within candidates (suggested edges as annotations) → top-k
```

Search becomes a ranker over a structurally justified subset, where a wrong answer is at least *related*.

### The asymmetry that drives ordering

Adding vector search later is **additive**. Getting the entity schema wrong is a **migration**. Therefore: design the schema now, keep retrieval swappable behind an interface, and let implementation order follow the evidence from Section 10.

---

## 9. The load-bearing risk — rewritten in v2

### What v1 got wrong

v1 claimed git-derivation meant "the graph builds itself" with "no new human work at all." That was overclaiming, and review located exactly where.

The chain is: **story → branch → PR → files → entities.**

The first three hops are near-lossless, because the existing SOP is already *one story, one branch, one PR*, with feedback arriving as commits on the same branch. That discipline — adopted for unrelated reasons — is genuinely valuable here.

**The last hop is not derivable.** Deciding that `LoginController.java`, `LoginValidator.java`, and `login.html` constitute `login-page` is a human judgement. That is ontology authoring, relocated one level down and renamed — the very failure mode the design claimed to dodge.

### What is actually true

Git-derivation does not eliminate authoring. It **changes what must be authored**:

| | v1 claim | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| What is authored | Nothing | The entity registry and its file mappings |
| Volume | — | Fewer than edges |
| Timing | — | Mostly upfront |
| Ongoing | — | Maintenance on every refactor |

That remains a much better cost profile than per-edge authoring. It is not free, and the paper now says so.

**Corrected claim:** the graph's *edges* build themselves from work already done, once the *entity registry* exists. Human effort concentrates in a bounded, upfront, maintainable artifact rather than an unbounded ongoing one.

### Additional failure modes

- **Hub-node poisoning.** A refactor or formatting PR touching 200 files creates `touched_by` hubs that destroy traversal usefulness. Mitigation: exclude PRs above a file-count threshold or labelled chore/refactor. Needed from day one.
- **Rename tracking.** Git follows renames only sometimes; heuristic and unreliable at scale.
- **Silent mapping decay.** Code moves without the registry moving. This is worse than noise, because it produces *asserted* edges that are wrong — see Section 4.6. The provenance fields exist specifically to make this decay visible.

---

## 10. Validation — rewritten in v2

v1 proposed one gate (git-link cleanliness). Review established that it measured the wrong thing and could not even run until the registry it maps into exists.

**Three gates, in order.**

### Gate 1 — Question mix (free, start immediately)

Log real agent queries from existing Claude Code sessions and classify:

- **Structural** — what calls this, what breaks if I change it, why was this decided
- **Content** — show me the existing pagination pattern, what does this config mean, is there similar validation elsewhere

v1 asserted structural dominance from introspection. Those are *an architect's* questions; a PR-review agent asks content and similarity questions too, and the graph answers none of them.

**Decision rule:** if content questions exceed roughly half the mix, graph-first is not wrong but it is the *second* feature, not the first.

This costs nothing and uses data already being generated.

### Gate 2 — Entity registry cost (the real unknown)

Author the registry for **one mature service**, timed honestly.

Measures: hours per service, entities per service, what fraction of files map cleanly, how much is ambiguous, how much a non-author could maintain.

**Decision rule:** extrapolate to the estate. If a service costs a day, the approach scales. If it costs a week, the office deployment never happens and the design must shift toward derived-only.

### Gate 3 — Derivation cleanliness (only meaningful after Gate 2)

Against a **mature repository with real issue-link discipline** — ideally a large open-source project, not the greenfield personal build.

v1 planned to validate in the environment where the design helps least: a new project with two small repos is the minimum-edge case. A good result there proves little; a poor result could wrongly kill a sound idea.

Measures: story → entity clean-mapping rate, hub-node frequency, rename survival, noise per useful edge.

---

## 11. The unaddressed gap — new in v2

Neither v1 nor the external review addressed **whether the agent will query well.**

The entire design assumes the agent knows *when* to reach for context and *what* to ask. The original SPARK experience named this as the least certain part — the concern was never that context could not be stored, but that the model would not know when to pull it.

A long design conversation has now covered the retrieval side thoroughly and the invocation side not at all.

This is a solved problem in the sibling project. DevTracker is deliberately **self-describing**: rich MCP tool descriptions delivered on connect, a bootstrap tool called at session start, and a repo-root instruction file the agent reads automatically. ContextRAG has no equivalent design.

**Required before build:**

- Tool descriptions written as the primary explanation — standing alone, stating when to call and when not to
- A bootstrap/orientation tool describing what is indexed and what is not
- Explicit guidance on the asserted / suggested / stale distinction, so the agent treats a lead as a lead
- A stated fallback when the graph returns nothing, so an empty result produces a file read rather than a confident guess

An excellent retrieval layer that is never invoked is worth nothing.

### Also uncosted

Both v1 and the review skipped operational economics, which in a bank are asked early:

- **Query latency** end to end, including traversal
- **Per-query LLM entity resolution** — cost and nondeterminism. "Same question, different entity resolved" is an audit conversation. Resolutions must be cached and logged. The names-in-prompt approach is fine at hundreds of entities and becomes its own token tax past a few thousand.
- **Re-index cost on merge** — how much work does a merged PR trigger

---

## 12. Named owners — new in v2

Every step in this design of the form *"and then a human does X"* is a cost paid by one person for someone else's later benefit. That is the exact failure mode Section 9 identifies, and it enters through several doors:

| Step | Owner required |
|---|---|
| Promote or reject suggested edges | ? |
| Mine `related_to` for missing verbs | ? |
| Maintain entity registry through refactors | ? |
| Act on the documentation-health metric | ? |

**Rule adopted:** any step without a named owner and a trigger is assumed not to happen, and the design must work without it. Unowned steps are deleted from the design rather than left as aspirations.

Where possible, attach the trigger to work already happening — registry maintenance in the PR that refactors, promotion in the review that surfaced the suggestion — rather than creating a separate curation activity nobody schedules.

---

## 13. Prior art — new in v2

**Aider's repo map** — the strongest validation and the strongest challenge. Builds a symbol graph from tree-sitter/ctags, ranks it, and uses the result to scope what enters the context window. Graph-based scoping of exactly this kind, with **no authored ontology and no entity registry**, built by roughly one person.

It demonstrates the Section 3 thesis works in practice, and poses the sharpest question in this document: **how much value arrives from the derived-only graph, before any entities, decisions, or authored edges exist?** If most of it, the entity layer is a refinement rather than a foundation. This directly motivates Phase 0 (Section 14).

**Backstage software catalog** (Spotify, CNCF) — entities declared in in-repo YAML, a registry with kinds and relations, ownership metadata. The storage format here is close to `catalog-info.yaml`.

*Important distinction:* Backstage operates at **service granularity** — ownership, lifecycle, service dependencies. The entity graph proposed here operates below that, at screens, concepts, and code clusters. It is a different tier, not a reinvention.

The useful move is **both**: if the platform team already runs Backstage, adopt it at service level (free credibility, free data) and build the fine-grained tier on top. **Action: confirm whether Backstage is deployed internally before designing around its absence.** Its documented lessons on entity identity, ownership, and registry decay are the field data Section 4.5 currently lacks.

**Microsoft GraphRAG** — the visible prior art, but note the difference: it *LLM-extracts* entities and relations from unstructured prose, paying the expensive derivation. The bet here is that code corpora make derivation nearly free.

**Sourcegraph code intelligence / SCIP, and Meta's Glean** — the industrial versions of that bet at scale. Worth studying for what a production code graph schema actually contains.

---

## 14. Phase 0 — the walking skeleton

Review and prior art converge on the same next step, and it dissolves the ordering argument.

**Scope:** derived code graph plus git story-linkage. No entity registry. No authored edges. No embeddings. Days, not weekends.

**What it answers:**

- How much value arrives before any authoring (the Aider question)
- How clean the story → branch → PR → files chain actually is (Gate 3, at file granularity, without needing Gate 2 first)
- Whether the query mix is structural (Gate 1, against something real)

**Why it comes first:** it converts both load-bearing assumptions from argument into measurement, and it is cheap enough that a negative result costs days rather than weekends.

**Sequencing conclusion.** The "mediocre everywhere vs excellent somewhere" dichotomy dissolves once tiered retrieval exists; the only question is what is built first. Phase 0 resolves it empirically rather than by preference:

1. **Design the schema now** — entities, edges, provenance, tiers. Migration asymmetry demands it.
2. **Build Phase 0** — derived-only, no authoring.
3. **Let Gates 1–3 decide** whether the entity layer or the prose floor comes next.

**Open before ticketing Phase 0:** whether it is a skeleton of the real system or a throwaway spike. That turns on the entity-registry question in Gate 2, and should be settled first.

---

## Appendix — status of the existing plan

An earlier plan exists: ten tickets (CTXR-1 → CTXR-10) across roughly four weekends, targeting Java 21 LTS + Spring Boot 3.4.x + MongoDB + an external embeddings API + a Python MCP server, with pluggable `CodeSource` / `TicketSource` / `DocSource` adapters.

**That plan assumes a vector-first Phase 1 and predates this reasoning.** Required revisions:

- Document model ticket → entities and edges first-class, with provenance fields
- Embedding service ticket → deferrable; replaced in Phase 1 by lexical search over prose sources
- New tickets → Phase 0 walking skeleton, ahead of CTXR-1
- New ticket → agent-facing tool descriptions and bootstrap (Section 11)
- Adapter interfaces → unchanged and still correct

No code has been written. This remains the cheapest possible moment to change direction.

pages.body:
# ContextRAG — Design Position Paper

**Status:** Concept stage. No implementation started. Seeking critical evaluation before committing to an architecture.

**Context:** A tech lead / solution architect at a bank is building a context retrieval system so AI coding agents can work with real understanding of an existing software estate. This document consolidates the design reasoning to date. It deliberately departs from the mainstream RAG pattern, and the purpose of evaluation is to determine whether that departure is justified or a mistake.

**A note to the evaluator:** The specific critique requests are in Section 10. Adversarial reading is wanted. Sections 8 and 9 contain the arguments the author is least confident in.

---

## 1. The problem

When a human tech lead works with AI coding agents at speed, context evaporates. Decisions scatter, architecture intent degrades, each agent session starts cold.

This was observed concretely. A self-hosted model at the organisation was given access to repositories, Confluence, and JIRA, and still produced generic output. The failure mode was **not hallucination** — it was genericness. The model could reach the data but did not understand how any of it related.

Two constraints emerged from that experience:

1. **Reaching ≠ understanding.** Access to sources does not produce ecosystem awareness.
2. **Token limits rule out brute force.** Loading whole repositories exhausts the context window before the task begins.

Single-service work is tolerable today. Multi-service work breaks down, because the agent understands one service's code but not the contracts between services, the Kafka topics, or the past decisions that constrain the current one.

---

## 2. What RAG actually buys — and what it does not

A common misconception needed clearing first, because it changes the design.

**Embeddings do not compress meaning for the model.** A retrieval embedding (e.g. a 1024-dim vector from an embedding API) and a language model's internal embeddings occupy **different vector spaces**. The retrieval vector is trained so similar documents cluster under cosine distance; the model's input embedding layer is trained so tokens land where the rest of its parameters expect them. They are not translations of each other.

Consequently the retrieval vector **never enters the model**. It is a lookup key and nothing more. What crosses into the model is always plain text, tokenised normally. Embedding cost is therefore *added*, never saved.

This eliminates "efficient representation" as a justification for RAG.

**What remains is the real justification: selection under a context budget.** With a thousand stories, they cannot all fit in the window. RAG's only job is answering *which ten go in*.

Once accepted, the design question stops being "how do we store context" and becomes **"how do we pick well."**

---

## 3. The core reframing: context as a graph

Context is not a pile of text. It is **a set of nodes and edges** — entities and the typed, directional relations between them.

The prevailing approach — chunk, embed, retrieve nearest — is correct for corpora with no structure. A software estate is the opposite. It has an abstract syntax tree, commit history, issue links, config wiring. The relations already exist and are machine-extractable.

Applying a technique designed for structureless prose to a corpus that is *nothing but* structure discards that structure and then approximates it back with similarity.

### Design by constraint, not design by prompt

- **Design by prompt:** hand the model everything and hope it infers the relations.
- **Design by constraint:** supply the relations. The model is told, not left to guess.

This is the thesis in one line, and the precise diagnosis of the observed failure.

**Consequence:** the unit of context is the **entity**, not the chunk. Chunks attach to entities; they do not float free. This is a foundation-level schema commitment — cheap now, expensive after implementation.

---

## 4. The model

### 4.1 Three node classes

| Class | Character | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Entities** | Internal, mutable, hold *current truth* | `login-page`, `credential-store` |
| **Events** — stories, decisions | Historical, immutable once closed | `VS1`, `CSS1`, `DEC-014` |
| **References** | External, stable, owned by nobody | `PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256`, `OAuth2`, `Kafka` |

Reference nodes have a property the others lack: **the model already knows what they are.** A reference node must not document the algorithm — it documents *this organisation's use of it*. That keeps them small enough to be affordable.

**Temporal separation** is what lets the system answer "what did we use before, and why did we change?":

| Question | Answered by |
|---|---|
| What does it use now? | Entity |
| When did that change? | Story |
| Why did it change? | Decision |

Reference edges attach to the **entity**, not the story — otherwise current truth must be reconstructed by replaying history.

**Boundary test for reference nodes** (without it, every library becomes a node and the graph drowns in noise):

> A reference node exists only if someone could reasonably ask **"why this one?"** — or if getting it wrong is a defect.

Argon2id vs PBKDF2 qualifies. `commons-lang3` does not; it is a line in a build file.

### 4.2 Edge vocabulary

The intellectual work is enumerating verbs and keeping the list brutally short. Every authored edge type is a tax paid forever.

**Derived — free, be generous** (from AST, git, build config):
```
calls · imports · produces · consumes · exposes · touched_by
```

**Authored — expensive, capped at five, treated as closed:**
```
implements · part_of · constrained_by · supersedes · related_to
```

`related_to` is the escape hatch and will absorb a large share of usage. That is acceptable and informative — when it dominates, its contents reveal which real edge type is missing. **The vocabulary grows from evidence, not from a design session.**

### 4.3 Language versus norms

- A **language** is enforced — grammar, validator, things that fail.
- A **norm** is social — convention, degrades gracefully.

Languages give guarantees but demand tooling before delivering value. Norms deliver value immediately and decay without enforcement.

The workable shape is **a thin language wrapping a thick norm**: closed, validated vocabulary; open human prose.

### 4.4 Storage format

**Do not invent syntax.** This is where such projects die — someone designs a notation and then spends the project writing a parser instead of building the system.

The consumer is an LLM, which reads semi-structured text natively. No parser is needed to make context legible, only a convention to make it consistent.

```markdown
---
context-spec: v1
entity: user-login-page
type: screen
edges:
  - implements: VS1
  - implements: CSS1
  - persists_to: credential-store
  - constrained_by: DEC-014
---

## What this is
The authenticated entry point...

## Why it is this way
Third-party login was deferred (see DEC-014) because...
```

YAML frontmatter in Markdown. Free parsers everywhere, git-diffable, renders in any viewer, readable by a model with no preprocessing. **Structure in the frontmatter; irreplaceable human knowledge in the prose below.**

Reference nodes carry parameters, because a bare name causes defects:

```yaml
entity: pbkdf2-hmac-sha256
type: reference
aliases: [PBKDF2, "SHA-256 hashing", sha256]
parameters:
  iterations: 600000
  salt_bytes: 16
  key_length: 256
authority: org-security-standard
prohibitions:
  - Never use bare SHA-256/MessageDigest for password storage — fast hash, GPU-crackable
constrained_by: DEC-014
```

The motivating example: "credential store uses SHA-256" is under-specified in a dangerous way. An agent given that will plausibly write `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")` for password storage — a security defect, since SHA-256 is a deliberately *fast* hash and GPU-crackable at scale. The real implementation is almost certainly PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (correct, FIPS-approved), casually shortened in speech. A human colleague disambiguates automatically; an agent does not.

The `prohibitions` field encodes what people repeatedly get *wrong* — knowledge that lives in senior heads, evaporates on attrition, and is cheap to write once.

**Version from line one** (`context-spec: v1`). The vocabulary will be wrong initially; the difference between a painful migration and an impossible one is knowing which files followed which rules.

### 4.5 Enforcement

A norm without a linter has a half-life of roughly six weeks in a large organisation.

- JSON Schema over frontmatter — unknown edge type fails CI
- Entity registry with aliases — `login-page` and `user-login-page` resolve to one node
- PR check — dangling entity references fail the branch

Roughly a day of work, and the difference between a living graph and a directory nobody trusts.

**Entity identity is a real hazard.** If names are free text, one concept becomes four nodes within a month and the graph quietly stops working. What an entity *is* — domain concept, code artifact, or screen — must be decided. Hedging across all three is fine on a whiteboard and fatal in a schema.

**Adoption constraint:** the whole specification must fit on one page. If it does not, it will not be adopted.

---

## 5. Sources have different structural character

Treating all sources uniformly is a mistake. Extraction strategy belongs to the adapter, not the core.

**Code repositories — most structured.** Services in a known language; edges from calls, imports, and the config portal wiring services together. Fully derivable, no authoring required. *Day-one caveat:* a new project with one service has almost no edges. The graph is correctly thin — nothing to infer, simply not much there yet.

**Ticket system (JIRA) — partially structured.** Some native links, but most stories are never linked to code because linking is optional and unenforced. Needs both derived edges where links exist and semantic candidates where they do not. This is where inference earns the most.

**Wiki (Confluence) — genuinely unstructured.** Prose, no native edges, and simultaneously the best per-project documentation store and the least connected. Its value is realised by proposing links *into* the structured layer.

**The bridging pattern:**

```
Confluence page  ──semantic──▶  JIRA stories  ──derived──▶  code entities
  (unstructured)   (suggested)     (partial)    (asserted)    (structured)
```

---

## 6. Asserted versus suggested edges

### The hard rule

**Cosine similarity never creates an edge.**

Closeness is not meaning. Two things can embed near each other and be unrelated; two things can be tightly coupled and embed far apart. An edge built on distance is a guess wearing the costume of a fact.

Similarity is symmetric and untyped. Relations are directional and typed. They are different objects. Collapsing them discards the exact property that makes a graph better than similarity search for structural questions.

### But inference still has a role

Most content is never explicitly linked. Nobody puts the wiki page ID in the ticket. A system showing only authored edges stays empty across most of the estate.

The resolution is not to ban inference but to **mark it**.

| Class | Origin | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Asserted** | Human-declared or git/AST-derived | Trusted, used as fact |
| **Suggested** | Semantic similarity | Candidate with a confidence tier, visibly distinct |

A human promotes a suggestion to asserted in one action.

> Semantics does not draw the graph. It **proposes drafts of edges** for a human to confirm.

This matters downstream: an agent must be able to distinguish "this service calls that one" (a fact to build on) from "this page probably relates to that story" (a lead to check). They cannot arrive looking identical.

---

## 7. Confidence scoring

Every edge carries a tier reflecting **how it was established**, not how high a similarity score was.

| Origin | Tier |
|---|---|
| Git-derived or human-declared | Highest |
| Explicit ticket link someone typed | High |
| Semantic candidate across sources | Moderate, labelled inferred |

**Primary use — ranking.** The tiering *is* the ranking function. Structured context surfaces first; semantic guesses follow; the agent can see which is which.

**Secondary use — a mirror.** The more valuable framing for leadership:

> The score measures the organisation's documentation health.

If retrieval is dominated by low-confidence guesses, that is not a tooling failure — it is the system reporting that the documentation is disconnected. The same number that ranks results becomes a quality metric to drive down over time. Better linking → higher confidence → better agent output. That is a roadmap, not just a feature.

**The trap.** A cosine similarity of 0.82 is not "82% probability of a real relation" — it is a distance. Bucket into high/medium/low; show no decimals. The moment three decimal places appear on a screen, someone treats them as truth, recreating the exact problem the design exists to avoid.

### The feedback loop

```
semantic proposes → human promotes or rejects → signal captured
                                                      │
                          thresholds tuned ◀──────────┘
```

Recorded per event: proposed edge and source pair, confidence tier at proposal, decision, actor, timestamp. Small, cheap, and must exist from the first version — retrofitting discards the first months of signal.

This yields per-source accuracy data (thresholds set from evidence, not guesswork), a metric that improves over time, and compounding value: each correction improves the next retrieval, unlike a static index that is exactly as good on day 400 as on day 1.

**This is not model training,** and overstating it would be a mistake. No weights change. What accumulates is a project-specific knowledge structure the model reads at query time. The learning is in the graph, not the model — which is a feature: inspectable (every edge has a visible origin), reversible (a wrong edge is deleted, not retrained away), portable (outlives any model), and attributable (answers trace to sources). A fine-tuned model offers none of these.

---

## 8. Why graph-first — the contested decision

### Why vector RAG is the default everywhere

Not because it is the best available structure, but because it is the most **generally applicable** one.

1. **The canonical case had no structure.** RAG was developed for open-domain QA over prose — encyclopaedias, support tickets, policy documents. There are no `calls` edges in a benefits handbook. Chunk-and-embed is not a compromise there; it is the only option.

2. **Vectors need zero authoring.** Point at a folder, get semantic search, model nothing. Knowledge graphs had their era — the Semantic Web, RDF, OWL — and largely failed at scale for one reason: someone must author the ontology, and that person is not the one who collects the benefit. Bad retrieval available tomorrow beats good retrieval requiring six months of modelling and organisational buy-in.

3. **A tooling flywheel locked it in.** An industry formed around the vector-shaped answer. "RAG" became synonymous with "embed and retrieve" through repetition rather than demonstration. Graph-based RAG exists and is active work; it is less visible because it cannot be packaged as a drop-in — it must be modelled per domain.

### Why this project may justifiably depart

Three conditions, rare in combination:

1. **The corpus is pre-structured.** AST, git, issue links. The graph is largely *derivable* rather than authorable — dodging the exact failure mode that killed the Semantic Web.
2. **The questions are structural.** What calls this. What breaks if I change it. Why was this decided. Vector search answers these approximately when an exact answer exists.
3. **Wrong answers are expensive.** A near-miss in a chatbot is a bad paragraph. A near-miss in a bank's PR review is a defect in production. Approximate retrieval is a much worse trade when precision is load-bearing.

> General solutions are correct when you do not know your domain. This domain is known — node types, edge types, and question shapes are all known. The generality tax buys nothing.

### The role vectors retain

Three legitimate roles, none of which involve defining relationships:

1. **As a property on a node** — enabling fuzzy English → node lookup, since a query like "how do we handle bad passwords on sign-in" matches no literal entity name. *Note:* at a few hundred entities, names plus one-line descriptions fit in a prompt, and asking the model to pick may outperform cosine similarity, because it reasons about the question rather than matching surface form. Embeddings may not be needed even here.

2. **As the floor for unmodelled territory.** The graph knows only what was authored or derived; pointed at an unmodelled service it returns **nothing** — and empty is the worst answer, because the agent proceeds blind, which is the original failure. Vector search over raw chunks returns *something*: degraded, unranked by structure, non-zero.
   ```
   Graph  → sharp, curated, grows slowly
   Vector → dumb, complete, covers everything from day one
   ```

3. **As a proposer of candidate edges** (Section 6).

### Scoping, not replacing

Joining every story attached to a long-lived entity re-creates the original problem — a blown context window. The graph **scopes** retrieval rather than replacing it:

```
query → entity resolution → bounded graph traversal
      → candidate set (~40 items, not 1000)
      → rank within candidates → top-k → context
```

Search becomes a ranker over a structurally justified subset, where a wrong answer is at least *related*.

### The asymmetry that drives ordering

Adding vector search later is **additive** — new collection, new index, existing queries untouched. Getting the entity schema wrong is a **migration**.

Therefore: spend the foundation budget on the graph model; keep retrieval swappable behind an interface.

### Practical shape

Phase 1 graph-first: entities, edges, stories, decisions, references in MongoDB, with `$graphLookup` for bounded traversal — avoiding the need to justify a new graph database to a platform team. Text search via the existing search index. Entity resolution via LLM.

This removes the embedding service and external embeddings dependency from Phase 1: one fewer external API, one fewer key, one fewer item in a security review — non-trivial in a regulated environment.

---

## 9. The load-bearing risk

### Authoring cost is what kills these projects

Ontology projects rarely fail because the ontology is bad. They fail because **authoring is a cost paid by one person while the benefit is collected by someone else, later, invisibly.** A design requiring every analyst to fill a "related entities" field will be honoured for two months and abandoned.

### Git-derived edges are the proposed answer

A story has a branch. A branch has a PR. A PR touches files. Files map to entities.

```
VS1 → LoginController.java, LoginValidator.java → login-page
```

This falls out of history that already exists — no new human work.

**Why it may be unusually clean here:** the existing SOP is already *one story, one branch, one PR*, with feedback arriving as new commits on the same branch. That discipline, adopted for unrelated reasons, makes story→code linkage far cleaner than at most organisations.

The intended shift:

> The graph builds itself from work already done. Human curation becomes **correction, not authoring.**

Correcting a wrong edge costs a fraction of creating a right one, and the feedback is immediate. That is a cost profile people sustain.

### But this is reasoning, not evidence

**The entire architecture rests on an untested assumption.** If git-derivation underperforms, the result is a system excellent on a small share of the estate and blind on the rest — whereas a vector-first build would have been mediocre everywhere.

**Mediocre-everywhere may be the correct shape for a first deployment.** A tool that answers all questions adequately may see adoption that a tool answering some questions excellently and others not at all never achieves.

**Stated validation gate:** test git-derived edge extraction on one real repository before hardening the architecture. Measure what fraction of stories map cleanly to entities, and how much noise the mapping carries.

### Secondary risks

- **Off the beaten path.** Every step from the default is a step to defend internally and debug alone, without Stack Overflow answers or vendor support.
- **Entity identity drift** (Section 4.5) — silent, gradual, and hard to detect until the graph is untrustworthy.
- **Cold start.** New projects have thin graphs by construction. The system is least useful exactly where greenfield teams might most want to try it.
- **Promotion may not happen.** The feedback loop assumes humans will promote and reject suggestions. That is another cost paid by one person for someone else's later benefit — the same failure mode the design claims to avoid, reintroduced through a different door.

---

## 10. Requested critique

Specific questions, roughly in order of how much they would change the plan:

1. **Is the graph-first departure justified, or is this a domain-expert over-fitting to a domain?** Section 8 is the crux. Argue the other side.

2. **Is the git-derivation assumption sound?** Section 9. What is the realistic clean-mapping rate for story → branch → PR → files → entities in a large enterprise codebase? What breaks it — refactors, renames, cross-cutting commits, squashes, monorepos?

3. **Is "mediocre everywhere" actually the better first deployment?** The adoption argument against graph-first may be stronger than the technical argument for it.

4. **Is the five-verb authored vocabulary right?** Too few, too many, wrong ones? Does `related_to` as an explicit escape hatch help or does it become a dumping ground that never gets analysed?

5. **Is the asserted/suggested split sufficient,** or does mixing trusted and inferred edges in one store cause problems not anticipated here?

6. **Is the claim in Section 2 correct** — that retrieval embeddings and model embeddings are non-interoperable, so RAG buys selection rather than representational efficiency? If wrong, much of the reasoning shifts.

7. **What is missing entirely?** Access control and permission propagation through the graph, multi-tenancy, index freshness and invalidation on merge, handling of deleted or renamed entities, and evaluation methodology are all unaddressed. Which of these is most likely to be fatal if deferred?

8. **Prior art.** Which existing systems solved this and what did they learn? Where does this reasoning duplicate or contradict published work on graph-based retrieval?

---

## Appendix — current implementation plan status

An earlier plan exists: ten tickets (CTXR-1 → CTXR-10) across roughly four weekends, targeting Java 21 LTS + Spring Boot 3.4.x + MongoDB + an external embeddings API + a Python MCP server, with pluggable `CodeSource` / `TicketSource` / `DocSource` adapters for portability between a personal build and an office deployment.

**That plan assumes a vector-first Phase 1 and predates the reasoning in this document.** It requires revision against Sections 3, 4, and 8 — specifically, the document model ticket must treat entities and edges as first-class rather than storing chunks with embeddings, and the embedding service ticket may be deferrable out of Phase 1 entirely.

No code has been written. This is the cheapest possible moment to change direction.
